newsitem.title: ITALY: Word "Mafia" hurts Italy's global image - survey.
newsitem.headline: Word "Mafia" hurts Italy's global image - survey.

text.p: "Mafia" is the word most associated with Italy in the eyes of foreigners, a label which does nothing for the image of a country which also gave the world "amore" and "dolce vita", a survey said on Wednesday.

The second Italian word most used by the world's press is "amore" (love) -- one of the few positive words linked to Italy, said the poll's creators, advertising agency McCann-Erickson Italiana and corporate communications agency Klaus Davi & Co.

Predictably, "pizza", "trattoria" and "dolce vita" numbered among the top 10 most popular Italian terms used in 60 publications monitored in the United States, Britain, Spain, Switzerland, Germany and France in the first half of this year.
But out of 3,021 articles studied, the Italian word most used was "mafia".

"From a linguistic point of view our country, the cradle of artists, navigators, poets and musicians, is sadly remembered today for having been the cradle of the most famous criminal organisation in the world," the researchers said.
"Unfortunately we shouldn't be surprised," Giuseppe Usuelli, chairman of the advertising agency, said in a statement. "Most of the news about our country relate to our misdeeds."

The survey, examining the image of Italy overseas which emerges from foreign press coverage, is aimed at Italian companies wishing to project their image abroad and will in future be carried out every six months, the agencies said.

The Italian company most often mentioned in the foreign press was loss-making state airline Alitalia, getting over 120 mentions, followed by troubled high-tech group Olivetti, private broadcaster Mediaset, confectioner Ferrero, spectacle frame maker Luxottica, clothing group Benetton and carmaker Fiat.
France emerged as the country most interested in Italian culture, followed by Germany and Britain, while the United States and neighbouring Switzerland manifested the least curiosity.
Articles about Italian fashion made up about 10 percent of the total monitored, with design house Gucci getting the most mentions, beating names like Gianni Versace and Giorgio Armani.

Sport, potentially an Italian strong point, in fact got little coverage, probably partly due to the national soccer team's early exit from the European football championships and the poor showing of Ferrari in Formula One motor-racing.

As for television, where the airwaves are dominated by state broadcaster RAI and private enterprise Mediaset, "the anomalous situation of a duopoly only confirms the negative stereotype that Italy is a country of bunglers with a lack of rules that is incomprehensible in the eyes of foreigners," the study said.
